## Background

Microplastics are a growing concern in the world today. Microplastics are 5mm or less in size and vary in shape and in composition (e.g. polyethylene, polypropylene, etc). The amount of these microplastics has been increasing over the years (Reddy and Lau, 2020), but not much is known about their long term effects on living organisms. Microplastics have been observed to acquire microbial biofilms under natural conditions (Ballesté et al., 2024).

Copepods are small zooplankton are some of the most important organisms in the food chain as they consume phytoplankton and they themselves are a very abundant, protein rich food source for animals as small as fish larvae to whales. Given their important role in foodwebs, how copepods respond to increasing exposure to microplastics will have strong effects on the a large portion of the food web. Previous studies with marine copepods have shown a potential hormetic curve (small amount of toxin has positive effect) with their CTmax when consuming a small quantity of microplastics (Zhang et al., 2025). Other studies have also pointed out that copepods are able to detect microplastics and avoid them when feeding with a success rate of up to 80%, even in the presence of a biofilm (Xu et al., 2022). These dynamics and the effects of biofilms may, however, vary across species (Fagiano et al., 2025)

Starvation also has adverse effects on copepod thermal limits. In one marine species, for example, it has been found that starvation significantly lowers thermal limits (Moreno and Sasaki, 2023). The effect of particle aging and biofilm formation may also depend on the nutritional state of the copepod. Under low-food conditions, the presence of a biofilm may provide some nutritional benefit to grazers (Botterell et al., 2020), offsetting the effects of starvation. Alternatively, biofilms may reduce the selective feeding behaviour, thus increasing exposure to microplastics.

## Methods

**Microplastic Incubation**

Set up shaking dry bath: click on button and dial, set rpm to 100sv, click dial in, then click thermometer button, set temperature to 26˚C, click dial in again, and click start to begin heating up. Wait for the shaking dry bath to heat up. Filter 200mL of collected pond water through 64 micron filter into 250mL beaker. Pulse microplastics on the vortex till the bottom of the container is clear. Take 3 eppendorf tubes and label CW for canal water, AW for autoclaved water and (-) for control and place in microfuge tube holder. Pipette 100uL of microplastics into 2 of the eppendorf tubes. Pipette 900uL of canal water into one of the tubes with microplastics and draw up 3 times into the pipette to mix the contents of the eppendorf tube. Pipette 900uL of autoclaved water into the other tube with microplastics and draw up 3 times into the pipette to mix the contents of the eppendorf tube. Pipette 900uL of autoclaved water into the empty eppendorf tube. Bring 3 eppendorf tubes to the centrifuge and place into the centrifuge making sure to balance it. Set the centrifuge to 6mins and 1000rpm. Take out 900uL of water from all 3 tubes while not disturbing microplastic pellets and dispose. Repeat procedure two times starting from: Pipette 900uL of canal water into one of the tubes with microplastics and draw up 3 times into the pipette to mix the contents of the eppendorf tube. Then repeat a third time and stop before the centrifugation. Add all 3 eppendorf tubes into the shaking dry bath towards the middle. Invert and shake all eppendorf tubes on Monday, Tuesday, and Thursday.

**Setting up Treatment Groups** 

Fill 12 120ml jars with 100mL of DIO water. Add 10uL of CW microplastics to 4 of the 120mL jars. Add 10uL of AW microplastics to 4 other 120mL jars. Add 10uL of (-) water to the last 4 120mL jars. Label 2 of the CW jars CW fed and the other 2 CW starved. Label 2 of the AW jars AW fed and the other 2 AW starved. Label 2 of the (-) water jars (-) fed and the other 2 (-) starved. Then for each pair of 2 jars that have the same label, label one A and the other B. Put the date on each of the jars.Take a plastic beaker and lower into copepod culture to collect animals. Grab a petri dish, the lid of a well plate, and a pipette. Pour contents from the plastic beaker into a petri dish. Pipette out female copepods into individual wells on well plate lids till you have 120 individuals. Take a light board, set it flat on the counter, and turn it on so the light is on facing up. Place all 12 of the jars onto the light board, setting them up 4x3. Then take a lid of a well plate containing the female copepods and place them under the dissecting scope. Using a pipette, take a female one at a time and place it into the closest jar to you. Move across the row and then move up to the second row and then the third row. All 12 jars should have 1 female copepod each. Repeat that process till there are 10 female copepods in each jar. Move all 12 jars to a styrofoam lid, and bring to the walk in chamber. Feed the 6 jars with the “fed” label 1mL of food using a pipette. Then randomize all the jars positions on the styrofoam lid. Place lids on all 12 jars loosely allowing oxygen to get in. Incubate for 7 days and on the 4th day feed all 6 fed jars again with 1mL of food using a pipette.

**Surivial Counting**

Take the styrafoam lid with the 12 jars back to the work bench. Grab 12 petri dishes and 12 petri dish lids. Take 1 jar, 1 petri, dish, 1 petri dish lid, a pipette, and a large beaker over to the dissecting scope. Pour about half of the contents from the jar into the petri dish and examine under the microscope. If any copepods are present pipette them from the petri dish and back in the jar. Once the petri dish is empty dispose of the petri water into the large beaker. Then pour the remaining contents of the jar into the same petri dish. Count the number of copepods dead and alive, and take not of the numbers. Remove the labe from the jar and place on the lid of the petri dish after counting is complete. Set the petri dish aside and repeat for every jar until all 12 are complete.

**CTmax**

Start filling in the log sheet on ctmax_assay.html for which water bath and thermometer you're using. Then move down to the group/tube layout. Label them as follows: Control - Fed, Control - Starved, MP - Fed, MP- Starved, Aged MP - Fed, Aged MP - Starved. Then scroll down and hit randomize. Fill the water bath with 2 L of water. Turn on the aquarium pump and the thermometer and place the probe in the water bath. While the water bath is adjusting, put 10 mL of DIO water into each of the 50 mL tubes. Arrange these in the tube racks in the water bath. Tubes should be numbered and should occupy the same position in the tube rack each time. When the temperature in the bath is about 26-27℃, move the thermometer probe to the tube assigned by the randomizer. Ensure that the probe is fully submerged throughout the duration of the experiment. Once the water in the tube is at 26-27℃, unplug the heater. Following the randomizer, place an alive and responsive individual copepod from the corresponding petri dish (keep note if A or B) into the assigned tube. Repeat this until there is the correctly assigned individual in each tube. Under each tube on ctmax_assay.html there is a section to add a note. Make sure to record whether the group was A or B in the notes section. Plug the heater back in to begin the temperature ramp. Monitor each individual closely throughout the ramp. As the temperature increases, occasionally shake the tube around while keeping it in the water bath to apply a stimulus. As the temperature continues to increase, shake the tube more frequently. If the copepod goes for more than 5-12 seconds without responding to stimulus it has reached CTmax. Record the temperature at the time of CTmax into the corresponding tube on ctmax_assay.html. Once all individuals have reached CTmax unplug the heating element and the aquarium pump and turn off the thermometer. Make sure to save the data somewhere/upload it.

**Statistical Analysis and Hypothesis Testing**

## Results

### Mortality Data

```{r}

surv_data |> 
  mutate(prop_mortality = num_dead /total) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = MP_treatment, y = prop_mortality, fill = diet)) + 
  geom_boxplot(position = position_dodge(width = 0.85),
               outliers = F) + 
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, position = position_dodge(width = 0.85)) + 
  labs(x = "Treatment", 
       y = "Mortality (proportion)") + 
  theme_matt_facets() + 
  theme(legend.position = "right")

```

```{r mortality-summary}
surv_data |> 
  mutate(prop_mortality = num_dead /total)  %>% 
  group_by(treatment_code, MP_treatment, diet) %>% 
  summarize(mean_mortality=mean(prop_mortality)) %>% 
  knitr::kable(digits=2)
  
```

```{r}

# Example GLMM with binomial response and a random intercept for 'cluster_id'
model <- glmer(
  cbind(num_dead, total - num_dead) ~ MP_treatment * diet + (1 | exp_rep/treatment_rep),
  data = surv_data,
  family = binomial(link = "logit")
)
# View summary and fixed effect estimates (log-odds)
summary(model)


# Perform omnibus test or pairwise comparisons across groups

car::Anova(model, type = "III") # Likelihood ratio or Wald tests

# Get estimated marginal means (proportions on the probability scale)
emmeans(model, ~ MP_treatment * diet, type = "response") |> plot()

```

### Thermal Limit Data

```{r}

ctmax_data |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = MP_treatment, y = ctmax_c, fill = diet)) + 
  geom_boxplot(position = position_dodge(width = 0.75)) + 
  geom_point(position = position_dodge(width = 0.75)) + 
  labs(x = "Treatment", 
       y = "CTmax (°C)") + 
  theme_matt() + 
  theme(legend.position = "right")

```

```{r ctmax-summary}
ctmax_data %>% 
  group_by(group_id, MP_treatment, diet) %>% 
  summarize(mean_ctmax=mean(ctmax_c)) %>% 
  knitr::kable(digits=2)
```

```{r}

ctmax_data |> 
  filter(group_id == "Control - Fed") |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = experiment_date, y = ctmax_c)) + 
  geom_point()

```

```{r}

ctmax.model = lmer(data = ctmax_data, 
                   ctmax_c ~ MP_treatment * diet + (1|experiment_date/file_source))

car::Anova(ctmax.model, type = "III")

```
